---
title: "Case Study: Reanalyzing a Published Randomized Experiment"
---

```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4.5,
                      fig.align = "center")
```

Simulated data show that a method works when its assumptions hold. Real data show
what happens when a study has missing covariates, censored outcomes, and a published
answer to compare against. This article takes one well-known randomized trial and
analyzes it end to end with EDI: the unadjusted estimate, a covariate-adjusted
model, a randomization test, a bootstrap, and every applicable asymptotic procedure
through `InferenceSuite`. It then compares the results with each other and with
the published effect.

It assumes you know the four-step pattern (design, assign, record, infer) from
[Get started](EDI.html). The [survival cookbook](cookbook-survival.html) covers
the same classes on simulated data.

```{r setup, message = FALSE}
library(EDI)
library(survival)   # the trial data and Kaplan-Meier curves
set.seed(20261117)
```

## The study

In the late 1980s, three US cooperative oncology groups ran a trial of adjuvant
chemotherapy after surgery for colon cancer. Patients whose stage III (Dukes C)
colon cancer had been resected with curative intent in the previous 1 to 5 weeks
were randomly assigned to one of three arms: observation only, levamisole alone,
or levamisole plus fluorouracil (5-FU) for one year. The outcomes were cancer
recurrence and death.

The first report (Moertel et al., 1990) found that levamisole plus 5-FU reduced
the risk of recurrence by 41% and the overall death rate by 33% (P ≈ 0.006) among
the stage C patients, and that levamisole alone had no detectable effect. The
final report (Moertel et al., 1995), with all 929 eligible patients followed for
at least 5 years (median 6.5 years), gave these figures:

* levamisole plus 5-FU reduced the recurrence rate by 40% (P < 0.0001) and the
  death rate by 33% (P = 0.0007);
* levamisole alone reduced the recurrence rate by 2% and the death rate by 6%.

The trial made levamisole plus 5-FU the standard adjuvant treatment for stage III
colon cancer at the time.

The data ship with the `survival` package as `colon` (LGPL (>= 2), so they can be
reproduced in documentation). The help page, `?survival::colon`, says the
data set is closest to the final report. It has two rows per patient, one for
recurrence (`etype = 1`) and one for death (`etype = 2`), and these baseline
covariates:

| Column | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `age` | age in years |
| `sex` | 1 = male |
| `obstruct`, `perfor`, `adhere` | tumor obstructed the colon, perforated it, or adhered to nearby organs |
| `nodes` | number of lymph nodes with detectable cancer |
| `differ` | tumor differentiation (1 = well, 2 = moderate, 3 = poor) |
| `extent` | extent of local spread (1 = submucosa up to 4 = contiguous structures) |
| `surg` | time from surgery to registration (0 = short, 1 = long) |

### Two arms and the design

EDI analyzes two-arm experiments, so we compare the two arms that carry the
headline result: observation (control, `w = 0`) and levamisole plus 5-FU
(treatment, `w = 1`). Dropping the levamisole-only arm is legitimate under
randomization. Among patients randomized to one of these two arms, which of the
two each one received was still decided by the randomization, so the comparison
remains a randomized comparison.

The primary analysis uses overall survival: time from registration to death, with
patients alive at last contact right-censored.

```{r data}
d = subset(survival::colon, etype == 2 & rx %in% c("Obs", "Lev+5FU"))
d$w = as.integer(d$rx == "Lev+5FU")
covs = c("age", "sex", "obstruct", "perfor", "adhere", "nodes", "differ", "extent", "surg")
X = d[, covs]
n = nrow(d)
table(arm = d$rx[, drop = TRUE])
colSums(is.na(X))[colSums(is.na(X)) > 0]
```

How was treatment assigned? The abstracts cited here describe a randomized,
concurrently controlled trial but do not give the allocation scheme, and
the `survival` help page does not either. Our primary analysis therefore treats the
assignment as complete randomization with the observed arm sizes: every split of
these `r n` patients into `r sum(d$w == 0)` controls and `r sum(d$w == 1)` treated
was equally likely. That is what `DesignFixediBCRD` draws when `prob_T` is set to
the observed fraction treated. In the
[Sensitivity check](#sensitivity-check-re-randomizing-within-strata) below we
re-randomize within prognostic strata instead and see whether the conclusion
changes.

## Exploratory look

### Balance

Randomization should leave the arms similar on every baseline covariate. The
table shows each covariate's mean by arm and the standardized difference (the
difference in means divided by the pooled standard deviation). A common rule of
thumb flags absolute values above 0.1.

```{r balance}
balance = data.frame(
  covariate = covs,
  control   = sapply(covs, function(v) mean(X[d$w == 0, v], na.rm = TRUE)),
  treated   = sapply(covs, function(v) mean(X[d$w == 1, v], na.rm = TRUE)),
  std_diff  = sapply(covs, function(v) {
    x0 = X[d$w == 0, v]; x1 = X[d$w == 1, v]
    (mean(x1, na.rm = TRUE) - mean(x0, na.rm = TRUE)) /
      sqrt((var(x0, na.rm = TRUE) + var(x1, na.rm = TRUE)) / 2)
  }),
  row.names = NULL
)
knitr::kable(balance, digits = 2)
```

```{r balance-max, include = FALSE}
worst = balance[which.max(abs(balance$std_diff)), ]
```

The largest standardized difference is `r round(worst$std_diff, 2)`, for
`` `r worst$covariate` ``. Imbalances of this size are what chance produces in a
trial of `r n` patients. They do not bias the unadjusted comparison, but they add
noise to it, and adjusting for prognostic covariates removes some of that noise.

### The outcome by arm

```{r km, fig.cap = "Kaplan-Meier estimates of overall survival by arm."}
km = survfit(Surv(time / 365.25, status) ~ rx, data = droplevels(d))
plot(km, col = c("grey40", "#1f77b4"), lwd = 2, xlab = "Years since registration",
     ylab = "Proportion alive", mark.time = FALSE)
legend("bottomleft", c("Observation", "Levamisole + 5-FU"), col = c("grey40", "#1f77b4"),
       lwd = 2, bty = "n")
s5 = summary(km, times = 5)$surv
deaths = tapply(d$status, d$w, sum)
```

The curves separate within the first two years and stay apart. At five years,
`r round(100 * s5[1])`% of the observation arm and `r round(100 * s5[2])`% of the
treated arm were alive. Over the whole follow-up there were `r deaths[["0"]]`
deaths among `r sum(d$w == 0)` controls and `r deaths[["1"]]` among
`r sum(d$w == 1)` treated patients.

## Recording the trial in EDI

The treatment was assigned decades ago, outside EDI. A fixed design accepts an
existing assignment through `assign_w_to_all_subjects(w_precomputed = )`: the
supplied vector becomes the design's assignment, while the design's own
randomization mechanism is still used to redraw assignments for the
randomization test. Setting `prob_T` to the observed fraction treated makes every
redraw treat exactly `r sum(d$w)` patients, as the trial did.

Survival responses are recorded as intervals: a death at time `t` is `ys = t`, and a
patient alive at last contact at time `t` is `y_Ls = t, y_Rs = Inf`.

```{r design}
des = DesignFixediBCRD$new(n = n, response_type = "survival", prob_T = mean(d$w),
                           verbose = FALSE)
des$add_all_subjects_to_experiment(X)
des$assign_w_to_all_subjects(w_precomputed = d$w)

died = d$status == 1
des$add_all_subject_responses(ys   = ifelse(died, d$time, NA),
                              y_Ls = ifelse(died, NA, d$time),
                              y_Rs = ifelse(died, NA, Inf))
colSums(des$draw_ws_according_to_design(3))   # each redraw treats the same number
```

`r sum(is.na(X))` covariate values are missing (in `nodes` and `differ`). By default
(`missingness_method = "impute"`) EDI fills them in by random-forest imputation
(`missRanger`) and adds a missingness indicator column for each affected
covariate, so no patient is dropped. The imputation uses only the other
covariates, never the outcome or the treatment, so the imputed values cannot carry
part of the treatment effect, and it is seeded, so the same data always impute the
same way.

## Analysis

All hazard ratios below compare levamisole plus 5-FU with observation, so a value
below 1 means the treatment lowered the hazard of death.

### Unadjusted and covariate-adjusted Cox models

`InferenceSurvivalCoxPHRegr` fits a Cox proportional hazards model. By default it
adjusts for every recorded covariate. Passing `model_formula = ~ 1` drops them,
leaving treatment as the only predictor.

```{r cox}
cox_unadj = InferenceSurvivalCoxPHRegr$new(des, model_formula = ~ 1, verbose = FALSE)
cox_unadj$num_cores = 1L
cox_unadj$compute_estimate()                      # log hazard ratio
cox_unadj$compute_asymp_confidence_interval(alpha = 0.05)
cox_unadj$compute_asymp_two_sided_pval()

cox_adj = InferenceSurvivalCoxPHRegr$new(des, verbose = FALSE)
cox_adj$num_cores = 1L
cox_adj$compute_estimate()
cox_adj$compute_asymp_confidence_interval(alpha = 0.05)
cox_adj$compute_asymp_two_sided_pval()
```

The default asymptotic procedure is the Wald test. The likelihood-ratio interval
inverts the partial-likelihood ratio test instead:

```{r cox-lr}
cox_adj$compute_lik_ratio_confidence_interval(alpha = 0.05)
cox_adj$compute_lik_ratio_two_sided_pval()
```

### Randomization test

The randomization test redraws the treatment assignment `r` times from the design
(here complete randomization with `r sum(d$w)` treated), refits the adjusted Cox
model on each redraw, and compares the observed estimate with that reference
distribution. It needs no proportional-hazards or large-sample assumption for its
validity under the sharp null of no effect for any patient.

```{r rand}
cox_adj$set_seed(1)
p_rand = cox_adj$compute_rand_two_sided_pval(r = 2000, show_progress = FALSE)
p_rand
```

The two-sided p-value can be no smaller than `2 / (r + 1)` (the observed
assignment counts as one of the draws), so with 2000 redraws it
says only that the observed estimate is more extreme than nearly every redraw.
EDI deliberately offers no randomization confidence interval for Cox-family
classes (see the [survival cookbook](cookbook-survival.html)); the bootstrap
supplies the interval.

### Bootstrap

The design is fixed and assigns patients independently of one another's outcomes,
so resampling patients with replacement is valid here.

```{r boot}
cox_adj$set_seed(1)
ci_boot = cox_adj$compute_bootstrap_confidence_interval(alpha = 0.05, B = 1000,
                                                        show_progress = FALSE)
ci_boot
```

### Other estimands

Three other classes answer related questions on different scales:

* `InferenceSurvivalLogRank`: the log-rank test, unadjusted and nonparametric,
  the test most trial reports of this era used;
* `InferenceSurvivalWeibullRegr`: a Weibull accelerated failure time model whose
  estimate is a log *time* ratio (above 0 means the treatment lengthened survival);
* `InferenceSurvivalRestrictedMeanDiff`: the difference in restricted mean
  survival time up to five years, in days, which needs no model.

```{r others}
lr = InferenceSurvivalLogRank$new(des, verbose = FALSE)
lr$num_cores = 1L
p_logrank = lr$compute_asymp_two_sided_pval()

wb = InferenceSurvivalWeibullRegr$new(des, verbose = FALSE)
wb$num_cores = 1L
wb_est = wb$compute_estimate()
wb_ci  = wb$compute_asymp_confidence_interval(alpha = 0.05)
wb_p   = wb$compute_asymp_two_sided_pval()

rmst = InferenceSurvivalRestrictedMeanDiff$new(des, tau = 5 * 365.25, verbose = FALSE)
rmst$num_cores = 1L
rmst_est = rmst$compute_estimate()
rmst_ci  = rmst$compute_asymp_confidence_interval(alpha = 0.05)
rmst_p   = rmst$compute_asymp_two_sided_pval()

# the same difference over the longest horizon both arms reach (the default tau)
rmst_full = InferenceSurvivalRestrictedMeanDiff$new(des, verbose = FALSE)
rmst_full$num_cores = 1L
rmst_full_est = rmst_full$compute_estimate()
rmst_full_p   = rmst_full$compute_asymp_two_sided_pval()
tau_full = min(tapply(d$time, d$w, max)) / 365.25   # years
```

### Every asymptotic procedure: `InferenceSuite`

`InferenceSuite` runs every inference class that applies to this design and
response type. As in the cookbooks, this call is limited to the asymptotic
methods with a per-class time limit; drop `methods` to also run every resampling
procedure at its full replicate count.

```{r suite}
suite = InferenceSuite$new(des)
res = suite$run_all_inference(screen = TRUE, plots = FALSE, num_cores = 1L,
                              methods = c("wald", "score", "lik_ratio"),
                              max_secs_per_class = 15)
```

Two rows need a word of explanation. "Strat Cox PH" is
`InferenceSurvivalStratCoxPHRegr`, which picks low-cardinality covariates
automatically and gives each of their strata its own baseline hazard. "Dep Cens
Transform" is `InferenceSurvivalDepCensTransformRegr`, a log-normal time model
fitted jointly with a model for the censoring times that allows the two to be
correlated. The Cox-type rows agree closely with each other. The two log time
ratio models agree less well, because they assume different time distributions
(Weibull versus log-normal) and handle censoring differently, but both point the
same way. Here censoring is mostly administrative: patients were censored because
they were still alive when follow-up ended, and
`r round(100 * mean(d$time[!died] >= 5 * 365.25))`% of censored patients had been
followed for at least five years. The independent-censoring models are the
natural ones for such data.

### Sensitivity check: re-randomizing within strata

Trials like this one often balanced assignment within prognostic strata. If that
was done here, the matching randomization test redraws treatment within those
strata. We do not know the trial's actual strata, so as a check we form four
strata from two prognostic factors recorded in the data, more than four positive
nodes (`node4`) and the time from surgery (`surg`), and pass them to
`DesignFixedBlocking` as explicit block identifiers `m`. Its redraws randomize
within each block at the same overall rate.

```{r blocked}
m = as.integer(interaction(d$node4, d$surg, drop = TRUE))
table(block = m, w = d$w)

des_blk = DesignFixedBlocking$new(n = n, response_type = "survival", m = m,
                                  equal_block_sizes = FALSE, prob_T = mean(d$w),
                                  verbose = FALSE)
des_blk$add_all_subjects_to_experiment(X)
des_blk$assign_w_to_all_subjects(w_precomputed = d$w)
des_blk$add_all_subject_responses(ys   = ifelse(died, d$time, NA),
                                  y_Ls = ifelse(died, NA, d$time),
                                  y_Rs = ifelse(died, NA, Inf))

cox_blk = InferenceSurvivalCoxPHRegr$new(des_blk, verbose = FALSE)
cox_blk$num_cores = 1L
cox_blk$compute_estimate()
cox_blk$set_seed(1)
p_rand_blk = cox_blk$compute_rand_two_sided_pval(r = 2000, show_progress = FALSE)
p_rand_blk
```

The point estimate is the same as above: the data, the imputed covariates and
the model are the same. Only the reference distribution changes, and the blocked randomization p-value, `r signif(p_rand_blk, 2)`, leads to the same
conclusion as the complete-randomization one, `r signif(p_rand, 2)`.

### Secondary endpoint: recurrence

The published 40% reduction refers to recurrence. Repeating the adjusted Cox fit
on the recurrence rows (`etype = 1`) gives:

```{r recurrence}
dr = subset(survival::colon, etype == 1 & rx %in% c("Obs", "Lev+5FU"))
stopifnot(identical(dr$id, d$id))    # same patients, same order
rec = dr$status == 1
des_rec = DesignFixediBCRD$new(n = n, response_type = "survival", prob_T = mean(d$w),
                               verbose = FALSE)
des_rec$add_all_subjects_to_experiment(X)
des_rec$assign_w_to_all_subjects(w_precomputed = d$w)
des_rec$add_all_subject_responses(ys   = ifelse(rec, dr$time, NA),
                                  y_Ls = ifelse(rec, NA, dr$time),
                                  y_Rs = ifelse(rec, NA, Inf))
cox_rec = InferenceSurvivalCoxPHRegr$new(des_rec, verbose = FALSE)
cox_rec$num_cores = 1L
rec_est = cox_rec$compute_estimate()
rec_ci  = cox_rec$compute_asymp_confidence_interval(alpha = 0.05)
rec_p   = cox_rec$compute_asymp_two_sided_pval()
exp(c(estimate = rec_est, rec_ci))
```

## All results together

```{r compare}
hr = function(x) sprintf("%.2f", exp(x))
ci_hr = function(ci) sprintf("(%.2f, %.2f)", exp(ci[1]), exp(ci[2]))
pf = function(p) format.pval(p, digits = 2, eps = 1e-4)
p_text = function(p) if (p < 1e-4) "p < 0.0001" else paste("p =", pf(p))

est_unadj = cox_unadj$compute_estimate()
est_adj   = cox_adj$compute_estimate()
ci_unadj  = cox_unadj$compute_asymp_confidence_interval(alpha = 0.05)
ci_adj    = cox_adj$compute_asymp_confidence_interval(alpha = 0.05)
ci_lr     = cox_adj$compute_lik_ratio_confidence_interval(alpha = 0.05)

results = data.frame(
  Procedure = c("Cox, Wald", "Cox, Wald", "Cox, likelihood ratio",
                "Cox, bootstrap CI / randomization p", "Cox, blocked randomization p",
                "Log-rank test", "Weibull AFT, Wald", "RMST difference at 5 years, Wald"),
  Adjusted = c("no", "yes", "yes", "yes", "yes", "no", "yes", "no"),
  Scale = c(rep("hazard ratio", 5), "(test only)", "time ratio", "days"),
  Estimate = c(hr(est_unadj), hr(est_adj), hr(est_adj), hr(est_adj), hr(est_adj), "",
               hr(wb_est), sprintf("%.0f", rmst_est)),
  `95% CI` = c(ci_hr(ci_unadj), ci_hr(ci_adj), ci_hr(ci_lr), ci_hr(ci_boot), "", "",
               ci_hr(wb_ci), sprintf("(%.0f, %.0f)", rmst_ci[1], rmst_ci[2])),
  p = c(pf(cox_unadj$compute_asymp_two_sided_pval()), pf(cox_adj$compute_asymp_two_sided_pval()),
        pf(cox_adj$compute_lik_ratio_two_sided_pval()), pf(p_rand), pf(p_rand_blk),
        pf(p_logrank), pf(wb_p), pf(rmst_p)),
  check.names = FALSE
)
knitr::kable(results, align = "llllll")
```

For comparison, the final report gave a 33% reduction in the death rate
(P = 0.0007) for these two arms (Moertel et al., 1995).

## Discussion

**Agreement with the published result.** The unadjusted hazard ratio is
`r hr(est_unadj)`, a `r round(100 * (1 - exp(est_unadj)))`% reduction in the
hazard of death, and the adjusted one is `r hr(est_adj)`, a
`r round(100 * (1 - exp(est_adj)))`% reduction. Both are close to the 33% the
final report gave. Every hazard-ratio, log-rank and time-ratio procedure in the
table rejects the null of no effect at the 1% level; the five-year restricted
mean difference is weaker, for reasons given below. The recurrence hazard ratio,
`r hr(rec_est)` (`r round(100 * (1 - exp(rec_est)))`% reduction,
`r p_text(rec_p)`), matches the
published 40% reduction in recurrence. Small differences from the published
figures are expected. The abstracts do not say exactly how they computed the
percentage reduction or which covariates their models used. The `survival` data
are also described as closest to the final report, not identical to it.

**Why the procedures differ where they do.** The procedures fall into three
groups, and the differences come from what each one estimates or how it
quantifies uncertainty.

* *Same estimand, different uncertainty.* The Wald, likelihood-ratio and
  bootstrap intervals for the adjusted hazard ratio are nearly the same. With
  `r sum(deaths)` deaths the partial likelihood is close to quadratic, so the
  large-sample approximations behind Wald and likelihood ratio agree with each
  other and with the bootstrap. The randomization p-values are bounded below by
  about 1/2001; they confirm the asymptotic p-values without adding resolution.
* *Different estimands.* The Weibull model reports a time ratio,
  `r hr(wb_est)`: under that model treated patients' survival times are stretched
  by about `r round(100 * (exp(wb_est) - 1))`%, with evidence as strong as the
  Cox models'. The restricted mean difference says treated patients lived on
  average `r round(rmst_est)` days (about `r round(rmst_est / 30.44, 1)` months)
  longer during the first five years (`r p_text(rmst_p)`). That is the weakest
  evidence in the table because it only counts time lived up to five years, when
  the curves had separated by about `r round(100 * (s5[2] - s5[1]))` percentage points; the gap kept
  widening after that (see the figure). Over the longest horizon both arms reach
  (`r round(tau_full, 1)` years, the class's default), the difference is
  `r round(rmst_full_est)` days (`r p_text(rmst_full_p)`). None of these are
  hazard ratios, so they should not be compared with the published 33% directly.
* *Adjusted versus unadjusted.* In a Cox model, adding prognostic covariates does
  not shrink the standard error the way it does in linear regression. It moves the
  estimate away from zero instead, because the hazard ratio is not collapsible.
  The conditional (adjusted) and marginal (unadjusted) hazard ratios are different
  estimands, and the adjusted one is usually further from 1 even without any
  imbalance.

**What covariate adjustment buys here.** In this trial, not much. The adjusted
log hazard ratio is `r round(est_adj, 3)` against `r round(est_unadj, 3)`
unadjusted, and the z-statistic grows from
`r round(est_unadj / ((ci_unadj[2] - ci_unadj[1]) / (2 * qnorm(0.975))), 2)` to
`r round(est_adj / ((ci_adj[2] - ci_adj[1]) / (2 * qnorm(0.975))), 2)`. With
`r n` patients and well-balanced arms, randomization alone already gives a
precise answer. Adjustment does help in another way: the number of positive
nodes and the extent of local spread are established prognostic factors in colon
cancer, and conditioning on them guards against chance imbalances like those in
the balance table above, so the estimate depends less on which patients happened
to land in which arm. It would matter more in a
smaller trial, where chance imbalance on a strong prognostic factor is more
likely.
